# Text fixtures — SynthID text-marking provenance record

Golden fixtures for the M3 SynthID check (`src/markproof/checks/synthid.py`).
They exist to hold that check to a standard the rest of the tooling landscape
does not attempt: EU AI Act Art. 50(2) asks whether machine-generated text is
machine-readably marked, and markproof answers that against a *running
endpoint* rather than against a vendor's self-declaration.

The whole matrix is generated by [`generate.py`](generate.py) and inventoried,
with every measured value and every SHA-256, in [`MANIFEST.json`](MANIFEST.json).

## The statistic, and why no model is needed

SynthID text marking biases token sampling using a keyed pseudo-random function.
`SynthIDTextWatermarkLogitsProcessor.compute_g_values()` recovers that bias from
a token-id sequence alone — it hashes each n-gram together with each watermark
key and looks the result up in a precomputed 0/1 table. The detection statistic
is the **mean g-value**: the average of those bits over all n-grams and all key
depths.

Two consequences shape this directory:

- **No language model is loaded anywhere.** A tokenizer turns text into ids and
  that is the entire dependency. `SynthIDTextWatermarkDetector` would require a
  trained `BayesianDetectorModel`; that is a separate, optional path and is
  deliberately not what these fixtures exercise.
- **The g-value ignores meaning.** It is a function of token ids, nothing else —
  not grammar, not topic, not fluency. This is why the fixtures can be, and are,
  synthetic token sequences (see [Honesty](#honesty-these-are-not-sentences)).

Unwatermarked text averages 0.50, because each g-bit is a fair coin. Fully
marked text averages ~0.78. `expected_mean_g_value(50257)` reports the
single-layer theoretical value of 0.75.

## Hard rule: every text here is our own production

No third-party text enters this directory — no scraped corpus, no benchmark
excerpt, no sample output from any model vendor. Thirteen of the fourteen
fixtures are token sequences synthesised by `generate.py` from a pinned GPT-2
vocabulary; the fourteenth (`unwatermarked-prose`) is a paragraph written by
hand for this repository. Nothing is downloaded except the tokenizer files
themselves.

## Tokenizer: `gpt2`, revision pinned

| | |
|---|---|
| id | `gpt2` |
| revision | `607a30d783dfa663caf39e06633721c8d4cfcd7e` |
| class | `GPT2Tokenizer` |
| vocab size | 50257 |
| gated | no — no HF token, no licence click-through |
| cache footprint | **2.8 MB** in `~/.cache/huggingface` |
| load time | ~7 s cold (first download), ~4 s warm — mostly the `transformers` import |

Only tokenizer files are fetched (`vocab.json`, `merges.txt`, `tokenizer.json`,
`tokenizer_config.json`, `config.json`). **No model weights are downloaded**,
which is the point: detection needs ids, not inference.

`bert-base-uncased` was considered and rejected. It lower-cases and strips
during tokenisation, so `text` would not round-trip back to `token_ids`, and
each fixture would quietly measure a different sequence than the one it
advertises.

The revision is pinned because it has to be. A re-upload of the `gpt2` repo
that changed the vocabulary would silently invalidate every measured mean-g in
`MANIFEST.json`, and nothing would fail loudly enough to notice.

### Round-trip safety

The check will tokenise the `text` field; the fixture claims a specific
`token_ids`. If those two disagree the fixture is worthless, so `generate.py`
asserts `tokenize(text) == token_ids` for every fixture and exits 1 otherwise.

To make that assertion hold rather than hope, the sampled sequences draw from a
restricted pool: one capitalised head token (`^[A-Z][a-z]{2,9}$`, 2 836 of them)
followed by space-prefixed lowercase word tokens (`^Ġ[a-z]{3,10}$`, 17 534 of
them). GPT-2 pre-tokenises on ` ?\p{L}+`, so each such token is its own
pre-token and re-encoding cannot merge neighbours across the space boundary.

## Watermark configuration — one config, fourteen texts

```json
{
  "ngram_len": 5,
  "keys": [654, 400, 836, 123, 340, 443, 597, 160, 57],
  "sampling_table_size": 65536,
  "sampling_table_seed": 0,
  "context_history_size": 1024
}
```

This block is repeated verbatim inside **every** fixture file and once more at
the top level of `MANIFEST.json`. That redundancy is deliberate: a g-value is
meaningless outside the config that produced it. Change `ngram_len`, the keys,
the table size or the table seed and every number in this directory becomes
wrong — not slightly wrong, but uncorrelated.

Depth is 9 (one g-bit per key per n-gram).

> **These are TEST KEYS.** They are the public example keys from the
> transformers documentation. In a real deployment the watermarking keys are the
> secret that makes the mark unforgeable. Committing them here is safe only
> because nothing in this repository ever marks real output with them.

## The matrix

Fourteen fixtures across four states. `expected_outcome` is what the check must
report; "why it matters" is the reason the fixture is not redundant.

### `watermarked` → `watermarked`

Built by running a 16-candidate tournament at every position: 16 continuation
tokens are drawn, and the one whose n-gram carries the most g-bits wins. This is
SynthID tournament sampling with a uniform proposal distribution in place of a
language model — the same selection pressure, so the same statistic.

| fixture | tokens | measured mean-g | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `watermarked-120` | 120 | **0.7864** | Shortest fully marked text still above the floor. The check must reach a verdict here without needing a wall of text. |
| `watermarked-240` | 240 | **0.7895** | The ordinary marked case, at roughly chatbot-answer length. |
| `watermarked-480` | 480 | **0.7792** | Long marked text. mean-g must not drift with length — a check that accumulates instead of averaging shows up here. |

### `unwatermarked` → `not_watermarked`

Tokens drawn uniformly from the same pool, no tournament, so every g-bit is a
fair coin.

| fixture | tokens | measured mean-g | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unwatermarked-120` | 120 | **0.5029** | Clean text at the length floor, where the statistic is noisiest. The false-positive case that decides whether `min_tokens` was set honestly. |
| `unwatermarked-240` | 240 | **0.5075** | The ordinary clean case. Must never be reported as marked. |
| `unwatermarked-480` | 480 | **0.4876** | Long clean text; converges tightly on 0.50. |
| `unwatermarked-prose` | 158 | **0.4827** | Real hand-written English, not sampled tokens. The others prove the statistic behaves; this one proves it behaves on text a person would actually send. |

### `weak-signal` → `uncertain`

**The state that justifies the whole matrix.** The 16-candidate tournament runs
at only ~40–42 % of positions, chosen by an independent coin flip per position;
the rest are drawn uniformly. This models text that is only partly machine
generated — a marked draft a human rewrote, a marked passage pasted into a
longer document, output from a model whose marking was partially disabled.

The resulting mean-g lands between the thresholds. There is no honest verdict
available, and a compliance tool that produces one anyway is manufacturing
evidence. These fixtures fail any implementation that rounds to the nearer of
"pass" and "fail".

| fixture | tokens | measured mean-g | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `weak-signal-160` | 160 | **0.6239** | Partly marked at short-but-valid length. |
| `weak-signal-240` | 240 | **0.6026** | Sits near the middle of the uncertain band, so it stays uncertain even if either threshold moves by 0.03. |
| `weak-signal-400` | 400 | **0.6156** | Long partly-marked text. Length removes the excuse that the ambiguity is small-sample noise: the signal really is intermediate, and more tokens will not resolve it. |

### `too-short` → `skipped`

| fixture | tokens | measured mean-g | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `too-short-3` | 3 | *n/a* | Fewer tokens than `ngram_len`, so `compute_g_values()` raises `RuntimeError`. The check must skip on token count **before** calling into transformers, not catch an exception. |
| `too-short-5` | 5 | **0.5556** | Exactly `ngram_len`: one single n-gram. A number is produced and it is pure noise. Computable is not the same as meaningful. |
| `too-short-24` | 24 | **0.5000** | A one-sentence reply. Plausible endpoint output, still far below the floor. |
| `too-short-64-marked` | 64 | **0.7796** | **The sharp one.** Genuinely watermarked, mean-g well above the upper threshold — and it must *still* be skipped. Length gating has to run before the statistic, which means the same gate that protects against false positives costs us this true positive. That trade is the honest one for an audit tool, and this fixture makes it explicit rather than accidental. |

## Calibration

Everything below is measured, not asserted. `python generate.py --sweep`
reprints it (16 seeds per cell, ~40 s) and exits 1 if the three populations stop
separating above the floor.

```
tokens    unwatermarked       weak-signal        watermarked
    40   0.463 .. 0.540   0.565 .. 0.698   0.765 .. 0.815
    64   0.463 .. 0.537   0.569 .. 0.667   0.757 .. 0.811
    80   0.472 .. 0.534   0.579 .. 0.658   0.756 .. 0.807
   100   0.475 .. 0.515   0.586 .. 0.657   0.764 .. 0.804
   120   0.479 .. 0.514   0.596 .. 0.642   0.765 .. 0.802
   160   0.471 .. 0.519   0.601 .. 0.652   0.767 .. 0.798
   240   0.475 .. 0.517   0.606 .. 0.648   0.774 .. 0.790
   400   0.476 .. 0.510   0.598 .. 0.631   0.778 .. 0.789
   480   0.477 .. 0.511   0.601 .. 0.630   0.777 .. 0.791
```

### Recommended decision rule

```
token_count < 100  ->  skipped
mean_g <= 0.56     ->  not_watermarked
mean_g >= 0.70     ->  watermarked
otherwise          ->  uncertain
```

**`min_tokens = 100`.** Each n-gram contributes 9 independent g-bits, so for a
text of *N* n-grams the clean-text standard deviation is

```
sigma(N) = 0.5 / sqrt(9N) = 0.167 / sqrt(N)
```

At *N* = 100 that is 0.0167, putting the lower threshold 3.6 sigma above 0.50.
The sweep shows why the floor cannot be lower: at 40 tokens clean text reaches
0.540 while weakly marked text reaches 0.698 — the populations have nearly met,
and that 0.698 would be reported as watermarked by any threshold at 0.70. Below
100 tokens no threshold placement separates the three cases, so the only honest
output is a skip.

**Lower threshold 0.56.** At or above the floor, the worst clean draw in the
sweep was 0.519. 0.56 clears it with room and stays 3.6 sigma from the mean.

**Upper threshold 0.70.** At or above the floor, the weakest marked draw was
0.764, leaving ~0.06 of headroom. Pushing the threshold higher would buy nothing
and would narrow the uncertain band, which is where the tool's usefulness lives.

Note that the old M3 planning figure of **0.40 as a lower bound is wrong** and
was never reachable: the statistic is bounded below by the fair-coin mean of
0.50 and, across every configuration measured here, never approached 0.40.

## Honesty: these are not sentences

Thirteen of the fourteen texts are **synthetic token sequences**. They read like
word salad — `"Charlie glam terrorist achie basal wrinkles merely invari …"` —
because that is exactly what they are.

This is correct for the purpose and it is not a shortcut. The mean g-value is a
function of token ids and of nothing else, so a fluent watermarked paragraph and
a nonsense watermarked sequence with the same length and the same marking
process yield the same statistic. Producing fluent watermarked text would mean
running a real watermarked language model at fixture-generation time, which
would make these files non-reproducible, slow, and dependent on a gated model
download — while changing the number under test not at all.

`unwatermarked-prose` is the one exception, and it is there precisely so the
matrix is not *entirely* synthetic: it demonstrates that ordinary human writing
measures 0.4827 and is not flagged.

What these fixtures therefore do **not** cover: whether marking survives
paraphrase, translation, or truncation by a real model, and whether real
production text from a marked endpoint tokenises the way ours does. Those are
integration concerns, and they belong to end-to-end tests against a live
endpoint, not here.

## Fixture format

Each `*.json` file is a single object:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | fixture id, equal to the filename stem |
| `state` | `watermarked` / `unwatermarked` / `weak-signal` / `too-short` |
| `text` | the text a check would receive from an endpoint |
| `token_ids` | GPT-2 ids; `tokenize(text)` must equal this exactly |
| `token_count` | `len(token_ids)` |
| `measured_mean_g` | measured at generation time, 6 decimals; `null` when shorter than `ngram_len` |
| `expected_outcome` | `watermarked` / `not_watermarked` / `uncertain` / `skipped` |
| `watermark_config` | the shared config above, repeated verbatim |
| `tokenizer`, `tokenizer_revision` | pinned tokenizer identity |
| `min_tokens` | the floor this fixture was judged against |
| `how_generated` | construction, including the RNG seed |
| `why_it_matters` | what breaks if the check gets this one wrong |

## Regenerating and verifying

```bash
python generate.py             # regenerate every fixture + MANIFEST.json, then verify
python generate.py --verify    # verify what is on disk, write nothing
python generate.py --selftest  # regenerate into a temp dir and diff SHA-256s
python generate.py --sweep     # reprint the calibration table above
```

Every mode exits **1** on any discrepancy. `--verify` re-derives the mean-g from
`token_ids`, re-tokenises `text` to confirm the round-trip still holds, checks
each measured value against its state's acceptance band, compares every file
against its SHA-256 in `MANIFEST.json`, and rejects a file that is on disk but
unlisted.

The acceptance bands used for verification are deliberately tighter than the
decision thresholds — `watermarked` ≥ 0.72, `unwatermarked` ≤ 0.55,
`weak-signal` within [0.585, 0.660] — because a fixture that only just clears
the threshold it is meant to demonstrate will flake the day somebody nudges that
threshold by 0.01.

### Reproducibility

Output is byte-identical across runs. Two consecutive full runs on 2026-08-31
produced these SHA-256 digests, and `--selftest` regenerates into a temporary
directory and diffs them:

```
296069e1e3039b685c3603060da02dd66109a52516d06b699c5f4d36702d2d2d  MANIFEST.json
242d242bd5d7040d5e37e2e92ccf07a1517ee0829cc29ed46760d1071bdad328  too-short-24.json
905c4b83d91fd2c4eb80db96217826dbbbae018ed449c663321886c1f9367d80  too-short-3.json
426aedcc6e79da569046884656edc2e5990ecaa9edd5fd0fb08e6f8cdf5cd87f  too-short-5.json
97f4c950b96fd50a531a0cbc8ec22d2ba9224294edf08af50e7d778abcf3ab02  too-short-64-marked.json
b023d363ee648e5b3950911b7daa2582d7a892879d7fa80b066651e918ec4e81  unwatermarked-120.json
66bb2f2338c20298d9a8723bec17aac4885fd86f1643f74d2dfec584341d1fc0  unwatermarked-240.json
882e9919a7b8c66fa784ba4131006883cd9a5c000d87d33f76fb426433652615  unwatermarked-480.json
0f668d852c7db81fb1c73a89624c045188caad2e69ced0b6900eae1b33646de7  unwatermarked-prose.json
4a43b0eac86e290a0f2a769b89fb9c28b2a2285fffdc82f04528b206d28c12ae  watermarked-120.json
be9176ec4222104d68bfacc616f562bf27221f50105ffe6b7a98d695bee281c6  watermarked-240.json
20e4a6a79d4054c4aa2b0102c09c79d045c5b5ba03449da4a8fe44b1bbd442f3  watermarked-480.json
12c2f49010b72897eb102491beb1d58f490f0118d882a04b71a3469de4787650  weak-signal-160.json
757ffbab646b6472d35fc0e6cb6af57a5b67f32a5eb49fc29c4012a2bbd92b9e  weak-signal-240.json
a58665e8eb3f38ccce3eb91977f586a6849d5c9f9b4c8c46637d73c1afed8a83  weak-signal-400.json
```

(These digests describe the fixture files at the revision that introduced them.
`MANIFEST.json` carries the authoritative per-file digest and is what `--verify`
compares against, so editing a fixture is caught even if this list goes stale.)

What makes byte-identity hold:

- token pools derived from a **pinned** tokenizer revision and sorted by token id;
- all sampling through `random.Random(seed)` with a per-fixture integer seed,
  drawn in a position-determined order that does not depend on which branch is
  taken;
- tournament ties broken by lowest candidate index — `torch.argmax` promises no
  such thing;
- g-values summed as **integers** and divided once, so no float accumulation
  order can leak into the stored value;
- JSON written through one encoder with fixed indentation, ASCII-only escaping
  and a trailing newline.

Unlike the C2PA media fixtures next door, nothing here involves a signature
nonce, so there is no reason for any file to be reproducible only in its
properties. These are reproducible in their bytes.

## Environment

Measured with `transformers` 5.16.1 and `torch` 2.13.0 on CPU (macOS, arm64).
`MANIFEST.json` records both versions. `compute_g_values` is integer hashing
against a seeded table and is stable across processes and instances; if a future
library version changes the hashing, `--verify` fails loudly on every fixture at
once, which is the intended failure mode.
